question: Which of the following is part of the Basis and Purpose of the Amateur Radio Service?
optionA: Providing personal radio communications for as many citizens as possible
optionC: Advancing skills in the technical and communication phases of the radio art
explanation: One of the stated purposes of the Amateur Radio Service is advancing skills in both the technical and communication sides of radio [97.1]. Ham radio is not meant to be a general personal radio service for the public, and contesting is an activity, not a listed purpose.

question: Which of the following frequency ranges are available for phone operation by Technician licensees?
explanation: Technicians have voice (phone) privileges on 10 meters from 28.300 MHz to 28.500 MHz [97.301(e)]. The lower part of their 10-meter segment, 28.000 to 28.300 MHz, is for CW and data, not phone.

question: Which amateur license classes are currently issued by the FCC?
optionB: Technician, Technician Plus, General, Amateur Extra
explanation: The FCC currently issues only three amateur license classes: Technician, General and Amateur Extra [97.9(a), 97.17(a)]. Novice, Technician Plus and Advanced licenses are no longer issued, though some older ones may still be renewed.

question: With which countries are FCC-licensed amateur radio stations prohibited from exchanging communications?
optionA: Any country whose administration has notified the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) that it objects to such communications
optionB: Any country whose administration has notified the American Radio Relay League (ARRL) that it objects to such communications
optionC: Any country banned from such communications by the International Amateur Radio Union (IARU)
optionD: Any country banned from making such communications by the American Radio Relay League (ARRL)
explanation: FCC-licensed amateurs may not exchange communications with any country whose administration has notified the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) that it objects [97.111(a)(1)]. The ARRL and IARU are amateur organizations and do not set these restrictions.

question: When may an amateur station transmit without a control operator?
optionA: When using automatic control, such as in the case of a repeater
optionB: When the station licensee is away and another licensed amateur is using the station
optionC: When the transmitting station is an auxiliary station
explanation: Every amateur station must have a control operator whenever it transmits, so it may never transmit without one [97.7(a)]. Even a repeater under automatic control has a control operator responsible for it.

question: When must the station licensee make the station and the station records available for inspection?
optionA: At any time ten days after notification by the FCC of such an inspection
optionB: At any time upon request by an FCC representative
optionC: At any time after a written notification by the FCC of such inspection
optionD: Only when presented with a valid warrant by an FCC official or government agent
explanation: The station licensee must make the station and its records available for inspection at any time upon request by an FCC representative [97.103(c)]. No advance written notice, waiting period or warrant is required.

question: Which agency regulates and enforces the rules for the Amateur Radio Service in the United States?
explanation: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) writes and enforces the amateur radio rules in Part 97 [97.1]. The ARRL is a national hobby organization, not a government regulator.

question: Which of the following U.S. amateur radio operators are allowed to contact the International Space Station (ISS) on VHF bands?
optionA: Only amateurs with a General class or higher license
optionB: Any amateur with a Technician class or higher license
optionC: Only amateurs with a General class or higher license, and NASA approval
optionD: Any amateurs with a Technician class or higher license, and NASA approval
explanation: Any amateur with a Technician class or higher license may contact the ISS, because its amateur station uses VHF and UHF frequencies where Technicians already have privileges [97.301, 97.207(c)]. No special NASA approval is needed.

question: Who may select a desired call sign under the vanity call sign rules?
optionA: Only a licensed amateur with a General or Amateur Extra Class license
optionB: Only a licensed amateur with an Amateur Extra Class license
optionC: Only a licensed amateur who has been licensed continuously for more than 10 years
explanation: Any licensed amateur may apply for a vanity call sign [97.19]. However, the call sign you choose must fit a format your license class is eligible for, so short call signs are reserved for higher classes.

question: Under which of the following circumstances are one-way transmissions by an amateur station prohibited?
optionA: Announcements of upcoming ham radio operating events
explanation: Broadcasting, meaning transmissions intended for the general public, is prohibited for amateur stations [97.113(b), 97.111(b)]. Some one-way transmissions are allowed, such as Morse code practice, telemetry, telecommand and brief announcements of ham activities.

question: Who may be the control operator of a station communicating through an amateur satellite or space station?
optionA: Only an Amateur Extra Class operator
optionB: A General class or higher licensee with a satellite operator certification
optionC: Only an Amateur Extra Class operator who is also an AMSAT member
optionD: Any amateur allowed to transmit on the satellite uplink frequency
explanation: Any amateur whose license allows transmitting on the satellite's uplink frequency may be the control operator for satellite contacts [97.301, 97.207(c)]. No special class, certification or AMSAT membership is required.

question: How often must you identify with your FCC-assigned call sign when using tactical call signs such as “Race Headquarters”?
optionA: Never, the tactical call is sufficient
optionC: At least every 10 minutes during and at the end of a communication
optionD: At the end of every transmission
explanation: Tactical call signs may be used, but you must still give your FCC-assigned call sign at least every 10 minutes during and at the end of a communication [97.119(a)]. A tactical call alone never satisfies the ID rule.

question: What do the FCC rules state regarding the use of a phonetic alphabet for station identification in the Amateur Radio Service?
optionA: It is required when transmitting emergency messages
optionB: It is encouraged when using phone emissions
optionC: It is required when in contact with foreign stations
explanation: Using a standard phonetic alphabet when identifying by voice is encouraged because it makes call signs easier to copy, but it is not required [97.119(b)(2)]. No rule makes it mandatory for emergencies or foreign contacts.

question: Which frequency is in the 6-meter amateur band?
explanation: The 6-meter band runs from 50 to 54 MHz, so 52.525 MHz is inside it [97.301(a)]. 49.00 MHz is just below the band, 28.50 MHz is in 10 meters, and 222.15 MHz is in 1.25 meters.

question: What types of international communications are FCC-licensed amateur radio stations permitted to make?
optionA: Communications incidental to the purposes of the Amateur Radio Service and remarks of a personal character
optionB: Communications incidental to conducting business or remarks of a personal nature
optionC: Only communications incidental to contest exchanges; all other communications are prohibited
optionD: Any communications that would be permitted by an international broadcast station
explanation: International amateur contacts are limited to communications incidental to the purposes of the Amateur Radio Service and remarks of a personal character [97.117]. Business communications are not permitted.

question: When is it permissible to transmit messages encoded to obscure their meaning?
optionA: Only when using a remote station during a contest
optionB: Only when transmitting certain approved digital codes
optionC: Only when transmitting control commands to space stations or model craft
explanation: Coded messages meant to hide their meaning are allowed only for control commands sent to space stations or to radio-controlled model craft [97.211(b), 97.215(b), 97.113(a)(4)]. Otherwise, amateur messages may not be encoded to obscure their meaning.

question: Who must designate the station control operator?
explanation: The station licensee designates who the station's control operator is [97.103(b)]. Neither the FCC nor a frequency coordinator makes that choice.

question: When are you required to transmit your assigned call sign?
optionA: At the beginning of each contact, and every 10 minutes thereafter
optionB: At least once during each transmission
optionC: At least every 15 minutes during and at the end of a communication
optionD: At least every 10 minutes during and at the end of a communication
explanation: You must transmit your assigned call sign at least every 10 minutes during a communication and at the end of it [97.119(a)]. There is no requirement to identify at the beginning of each contact or during every transmission.

question: How do you receive official notification of your new license and call sign after passing the exam?
optionA: Email from the FCC with a link to download the license grant
optionB: USPS First-Class Mail from the FCC
optionC: Email from the lead volunteer examiner
optionD: USPS First-Class Mail from the lead volunteer examiner
explanation: The FCC no longer mails paper licenses; it sends an email with a link to download your official license grant [97.23]. The volunteer examiners only submit your exam results, they do not issue the license.

question: Which amateur band includes 146.52 MHz?
explanation: The 2-meter band covers 144 to 148 MHz, so 146.52 MHz falls inside it [97.301(a)]. In fact, 146.52 MHz is the national FM simplex calling frequency for 2 meters.

question: What may happen if the FCC is unable to reach you by email?
optionA: Fine and suspension of operator license
optionB: Revocation of the station license or suspension of the operator license
optionC: Revocation of access to the license record in the FCC system
optionD: Nothing; there is no such requirement
explanation: Licensees must keep a valid email address on file with the FCC, and if FCC correspondence cannot reach you, the FCC may revoke your station license or suspend your operator license [97.23]. So the requirement is real and the penalty can be serious.

question: Under what conditions is an amateur station authorized to transmit music using a phone emission?
optionA: When incidental to an authorized retransmission of manned spacecraft communications
optionB: When the music produces no spurious emissions
optionC: When transmissions are limited to less than three minutes per hour
optionD: When the music is transmitted above 1280 MHz
explanation: Music may be transmitted only when it is incidental to an authorized retransmission of manned spacecraft communications [97.113(a)(4), 97.113(c)]. Low spurious emissions, short time limits or higher frequencies do not make music allowed.

question: What determines the transmitting frequency privileges of an amateur station?
optionA: The frequency authorized by the frequency coordinator
optionB: The frequencies printed on the license grant
optionC: The highest class of operator license held by anyone on the premises
optionD: The class of operator license held by the control operator
explanation: A station's transmitting privileges depend on the license class held by its control operator [97.103(b)]. Frequencies are not printed on the license grant, and licenses held by other people present do not count.

question: What language must you use for identification when using a phone emission?
optionA: Any language recognized by the United Nations
optionB: Any language recognized by the ITU
explanation: When identifying by voice, you must use the English language [97.119(b)(2)]. Your conversation may be in another language, but the station identification must be in English.

question: What proves that the FCC has issued an operator/primary license grant?
optionA: A printed copy of the certificate of successful completion of examination
optionB: An email notification from the NCVEC granting the license
optionC: The license appears in the FCC ULS database
explanation: A license is officially granted when it appears in the FCC's Universal Licensing System (ULS) database [97.7]. A certificate of completing the exam or an email from someone other than the FCC does not prove the license was issued.

question: Which of the following bands include frequencies where Technicians are authorized to use digital modes such as FT8?
explanation: Technicians may use data modes such as FT8 on all three bands listed: in their 10-meter segment and on the 6-meter and 2-meter bands [97.301, 97.305]. That is why all the choices are correct.

question: Which of the following is a valid Group D call sign format for Technician class?
explanation: KF1XXX is a Group D call sign: two letters (starting with K or W), a digit, then three letters, which is the format available to Technician licensees. KA1X and W1XX are short Group A formats reserved for Amateur Extra licensees.

question: When may amateur radio operators use their stations to notify other amateurs of the availability of equipment for sale or trade?
optionB: When the equipment is not the personal property of either the station licensee, or the control operator, or their close relatives
optionC: When no profit is made on the sale
optionD: When selling amateur radio equipment and not on a regular basis
explanation: You may advertise amateur radio equipment for sale or trade on the air as long as you are not doing it on a regular basis, meaning it is not a business [97.113(a)(3)(ii)]. The exception applies to amateur equipment only.

question: What is an amateur station’s control point?
optionA: The location of the station’s transmitting antenna
optionB: The location of the station’s transmitting apparatus
optionC: The location at which the control operator function is performed
optionD: The mailing address of the station licensee
explanation: The control point is wherever the control operator actually performs the control function [97.3(a)(14)]. It need not be where the antenna or the transmitter is located.

question: What method of call sign identification is required for a station transmitting phone signals?
optionA: Send the call sign followed by the indicator RPT
optionB: Send the call sign using a CW or phone emission
optionC: Send the call sign followed by the indicator R
optionD: Send the call sign using only a phone emission
explanation: A station transmitting phone may identify using either a voice (phone) emission or CW (Morse code) [97.119(b)(2)]. That is why choice D, phone only, is wrong.

question: On which of the following HF frequencies can automatically controlled amateur propagation beacons be found?
optionA: Anywhere in the Technician portion of 10 meters
optionB: Anywhere, if they are registered with the FCC
optionC: In a specific portion of each of the HF Technician bands
optionD: On ten meters, between 28.200 MHz and 28.300 MHz
explanation: Automatically controlled propagation beacons on HF are limited to the 28.200 to 28.300 MHz segment of 10 meters [97.203(d)]. They are not allowed anywhere else in the Technician HF bands, and FCC registration does not change that.

question: On which HF bands does a Technician class operator have phone privileges?
explanation: On HF, Technicians have phone privileges only on 10 meters, from 28.300 to 28.500 MHz [97.301(e), 97.305]. Their privileges on 80, 40 and 15 meters are CW only, not phone.

question: Which of the following statements is true about using your amateur radio license when operating aboard a vessel or craft in international waters?
optionA: Amateur operation is prohibited in international waters
optionB: You may only operate during maritime emergencies
optionC: You need special FCC authorization for maritime mobile operation
optionD: You may operate from a US-documented vessel with the master's permission
explanation: You may operate with your FCC amateur license aboard a US-documented vessel or craft in international waters, as long as the master of the vessel gives permission [97.5(a)(2), 97.11(a)]. No special FCC authorization is needed.

question: What, if any, are the restrictions concerning transmission of language that may be considered indecent or obscene?
optionA: The FCC maintains a list of words that are not permitted to be used on amateur frequencies
optionC: The International Telecommunications Union (ITU) maintains a list of words that are not permitted to be used on amateur frequencies
explanation: Indecent or obscene language is prohibited on amateur radio [97.113(a)(4)]. There is no official list of banned words from the FCC or ITU; all such language is simply not allowed.

question: When, other than during an emergency, may a Technician class licensee be the control operator of a station operating in an Amateur Extra Class band segment?
optionB: When designated as the control operator by an Amateur Extra Class licensee
optionC: As part of a multi-operator contest team
optionD: When using a club station whose trustee holds an Amateur Extra Class license
explanation: Outside of emergencies, a Technician may never act as control operator in an Amateur Extra band segment [97.301]. The control operator's own license class sets the privileges, regardless of who owns the station or designates them.

question: Which of the following self-assigned indicators are acceptable when using a phone transmission?
explanation: When adding a self-assigned indicator by voice, you may separate it from your call sign with any suitable word such as stroke, slant or slash [97.119(c)]. All three choices are acceptable.

question: What is the FCC Part 97 definition of a space station?
optionC: An amateur station located more than 50 km above Earth's surface
optionD: An amateur station using amateur radio satellites for relay of signals
explanation: Part 97 defines a space station as an amateur station located more than 50 km above the Earth's surface [97.3(a)(41)]. It does not have to be a satellite, and a ground station that uses a satellite is not itself a space station.

question: Which of the following VHF/UHF band segments are limited to CW only?
optionA: 50.0 MHz to 50.1 MHz and 144.0 MHz to 144.1 MHz
optionB: 219 MHz to 220 MHz and 420.0 MHz to 420.1 MHz
explanation: The bottom 100 kHz of 6 meters (50.0 to 50.1 MHz) and of 2 meters (144.0 to 144.1 MHz) are reserved for CW only [97.305(a), (c)]. The other segments listed allow other modes as well.

question: How long before the expiration date may an amateur radio license renewal be requested?
explanation: You may request renewal of your amateur license up to 90 days before it expires [97.21, 1.949]. Renewals are filed through the FCC's online license system.

question: Which of the following is an example of an auxiliary station?
optionA: A station sending one-way transmissions between a remote repeater receiver and the main repeater transmitter
optionB: A backup radio for emergency use in case the main station radio fails
optionC: A station used in the Military Auxiliary Radio System for linking government and amateur stations in a digital network
optionD: A second station utilized in multi-operator contest stations
explanation: An auxiliary station handles point-to-point links within an amateur system, such as sending a repeater's signal from a remote receiver to the main repeater transmitter [97.113(d), 97.201(e)]. A backup radio or second contest station is not an auxiliary station.

question: When the control operator is not the station licensee, who is responsible for the proper operation of the station?
optionA: All licensed amateurs who are present at the operation
optionD: The control operator and the station licensee
explanation: When someone other than the licensee is the control operator, both the control operator and the station licensee are responsible for proper operation [97.103(a)]. Responsibility is shared, not passed entirely to one person.

question: Which of the following restrictions apply when a non-licensed person speaks to a foreign amateur radio station via a station under the control of an FCC-licensed amateur radio operator?
optionA: The person must be a U.S. citizen
optionB: The foreign station must be in a country with which the U.S. has a third-party agreement
optionC: The licensed control operator must do the station identification
explanation: A non-licensed person may talk with a foreign amateur station only if that country has a third-party agreement with the United States [97.115(a)(2)]. The third party does not need to be a U.S. citizen.

question: Who recommends transmit/receive channels for repeater and auxiliary stations?
optionA: A Frequency Spectrum Manager appointed by the FCC
optionB: A Volunteer Frequency Coordinator recognized by local amateurs
explanation: Repeater and auxiliary channels are recommended by a Volunteer Frequency Coordinator recognized by local amateurs [97.3(a)(22)]. The FCC does not assign repeater channels; coordination is a volunteer, local process.

question: How are US amateurs restricted in segments of bands where the Amateur Radio Service is secondary?
optionA: U.S. amateurs may find non-amateur stations in those segments, and must avoid interfering with them
optionB: U.S. amateurs must give foreign amateur stations priority in those segments
optionC: International communications are not permitted in those segments
optionD: Digital transmissions are not permitted in those segments
explanation: Where amateurs are secondary users, other (non-amateur) services have priority, so you may hear their stations and must not cause them interference [97.303]. It has nothing to do with giving foreign hams priority or banning certain modes.

question: What is the normal term for an FCC-issued amateur radio license?
explanation: An FCC amateur radio license is normally valid for ten years [97.25]. It can be renewed, so a license is not issued for life.

question: In which of the following circumstances may the control operator of an amateur station receive compensation for operating that station?
optionA: When the communication is related to the sale of amateur equipment by the control operator's employer
optionB: When the communication is a part of classroom instruction at an educational institution
optionC: When the communication is made to obtain emergency information for a local broadcast station
explanation: A teacher may be paid for operating an amateur station when it is part of classroom instruction at an educational institution [97.113(a)(3)(iii)]. Amateurs generally may not be paid for operating, and sales for an employer or news gathering for a broadcaster do not qualify.

question: Which of the following is an example of automatic control?
optionB: Controlling a station over the internet
optionC: Using a computer or other device to send CW automatically
optionD: Using a computer or other device to identify automatically
explanation: Repeater operation is the classic example of automatic control, where the station operates without the control operator at the control point [97.3(a)(6), 97.205(d)]. Operating over the internet is remote control, and automatic CW or ID devices are just station accessories.

question: What is the definition of third-party communications?
optionA: A message from a control operator to another amateur station control operator on behalf of another person
optionB: Amateur radio communications where three stations are in communications with one another
optionC: Operation when the transmitting equipment is licensed to a person other than the control operator
optionD: Temporary authorization for an unlicensed person to transmit on the amateur bands for technical experiments
explanation: Third-party communication is a message sent by one station's control operator to another station's control operator on behalf of another person, the third party [97.3(a)(47)]. It does not mean three stations talking together.

question: Who selects a Frequency Coordinator?
optionA: The FCC Office of Spectrum Management and Coordination Policy
optionB: The local chapter of the Office of National Council of Independent Frequency Coordinators
optionC: Amateur operators in a local or regional area whose stations are eligible to be repeater or auxiliary stations
explanation: A Frequency Coordinator is chosen by the amateur operators in a local or regional area whose stations are eligible to be repeater or auxiliary stations [97.3(a)(22)]. The FCC does not appoint coordinators.

question: Why should you not set your transmit frequency to be exactly at the edge of an amateur band or sub-band?
optionA: To allow for calibration error in the transmitter frequency display
optionB: So that modulation sidebands do not extend beyond the band edge
optionC: To allow for transmitter frequency drift
explanation: Your signal occupies more than the single frequency on the dial, and the dial reading may be slightly off or drift, so transmitting right at a band edge could put part of your signal outside the band [97.101(a), 97.301(a-e)]. Calibration error, sidebands and drift are all valid reasons, so all choices are correct.

question: What is the grace period for renewal if an amateur license expires?
explanation: If your license expires, you have a two-year grace period in which you may still renew it [97.21(a)(b)]. After that, you would have to take the exam again.

question: When may amateur stations transmit information in support of broadcasting, program production, or news gathering, assuming no other means is available?
optionA: When such communications are directly related to the immediate safety of human life or protection of property
optionB: When broadcasting communications to or from the space shuttle
optionC: Where non-commercial programming is gathered and supplied exclusively to the National Public Radio network
explanation: Amateurs may help broadcasting or news gathering only when the communications relate directly to the immediate safety of human life or protection of property and no other means is available [97.113]. Otherwise, supporting broadcasting is not allowed.

question: Which amateur stations may be remotely controlled?
explanation: Any amateur station may be remotely controlled [97.109(c)]. Remote control is not limited to repeaters, automatic stations or digital stations.

question: What type of amateur station simultaneously retransmits the signal of another amateur station on a different channel or channels?
explanation: A repeater station receives a signal and simultaneously retransmits it on a different channel or channels [97.3(a)(40)]. Beacons and message forwarding stations do not repeat signals in real time this way.

question: Besides an FCC-issued amateur operator license, what is required to be the control operator of a Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service (RACES) Station?
optionA: A written recommendation by the local ARRL Emergency Coordinator
optionB: Membership in the Amateur Radio Emergency Service (ARES)
optionC: Certification of current enrollment by a civil defense organization
explanation: To be the control operator of a RACES station you need, besides your license, certification that you are currently enrolled in a civil defense organization [97.407(a)]. ARES membership or an ARRL recommendation does not satisfy this rule.

question: Where may SSB phone be used in amateur bands above 50 MHz?
optionA: Only in sub-bands allocated to General class or higher licensees
optionC: In at least some segment of all these bands
optionD: On any band if the power is limited to 25 watts
explanation: Single sideband (SSB) phone is permitted in at least some segment of every amateur band above 50 MHz [97.305(c)]. It is not limited to General class sub-bands, repeaters, or a particular power level.

question: How soon after passing the examination for your first amateur radio license may you transmit on the amateur radio bands?
optionA: Immediately on receiving your Certificate of Successful Completion of Examination (CSCE)
optionB: As soon as your operator/station license grant appears on the ARRL website
optionC: As soon as your operator/station license grant appears in the FCC’s license database
optionD: As soon as you receive your license in the mail from the FCC
explanation: A new licensee may begin transmitting as soon as the license grant appears in the FCC's license database (ULS) [97.5(a)]. Passing the exam and receiving a CSCE does not by itself let someone without a license transmit.

question: How does the FCC define broadcasting for the Amateur Radio Service?
optionB: Any transmission made by the licensed station
optionC: Transmission of messages directed only to amateur operators
optionD: Transmissions intended for reception by the general public
explanation: In amateur radio rules, broadcasting means transmissions intended for reception by the general public [97.3(a)(10)]. Normal two-way contacts or messages to other hams are not broadcasting.

question: Which of the following is an example of remote control as defined in Part 97?
optionB: Operating the station over the internet
optionC: Controlling a model aircraft, boat, or car by amateur radio
explanation: Operating your station over the internet from another location is remote control as defined in Part 97 [97.3(a)(39)]. Controlling a model aircraft or car by radio is telecommand of a model craft, not remote control of an amateur station.

question: Who is accountable if a repeater inadvertently retransmits communications that violate the FCC rules?
optionA: The control operator of the originating station
optionB: The control operator of the repeater
optionD: Both the originating station and the repeater owner
explanation: If a repeater accidentally retransmits a rule violation, the control operator of the station that originated the signal is accountable [97.205(g)]. The repeater's control operator is not held responsible for an inadvertent retransmission.

question: Which of the following is prohibited?
optionA: International communications on VHF bands and higher frequencies
explanation: No amateur station may willfully or maliciously interfere with, or cause interference to, any radio communication or signal [97.101(d)]. International contacts on VHF and digital third-party traffic are both permitted.

question: What is the maximum peak envelope power output for Technician class operators in their HF band segments?
explanation: Technicians are limited to 200 watts peak envelope power (PEP) output in their HF band segments [97.313]. The 1500-watt limit applies to Technicians only above 30 MHz.

question: If your license has expired and is still within the allowable grace period, may you continue to transmit on the amateur radio bands?
optionA: Yes, for up to two years
optionB: Yes, as soon as you apply for renewal
optionC: Yes, for up to one year
optionD: No, you must wait until the license has been renewed
explanation: No, you may not transmit during the grace period; it only gives you time to renew, and you must wait until the renewal is granted [97.21(b)]. The two-year grace period is a common trap in choice A.

question: When may an amateur station transmit without identifying on the air?
optionA: When the transmissions are of a brief nature to make station adjustments
optionC: When the transmitted power level is below 0.1 watt
optionD: When transmitting signals to control model craft
explanation: Signals used to control a model craft (a radio-controlled model plane, boat or car) do not need station identification [97.215]. Brief test transmissions, unmodulated signals and very low power transmissions still need to be identified.

question: What is a control operator as defined in Part 97?
optionA: The person speaking or otherwise communicating messages over an amateur station
optionB: The person who is the licensee of an amateur station
optionC: An amateur operator identified in the FCC database as responsible for transmissions and FCC rules compliance at a station license location
optionD: An amateur operator designated by the licensee of a station to be responsible for transmissions and FCC rules compliance at that station
explanation: A control operator is an amateur operator designated by the station licensee to be responsible for the transmissions and rules compliance of that station [97.3(a)(13)]. The person speaking is not necessarily the control operator, and the FCC database does not list control operators.

question: Which of the following is a requirement for the issuance of a club station license grant?
optionA: The trustee must have an Amateur Extra Class operator license grant
optionB: The club must have at least four members
optionC: The club must be registered with the American Radio Relay League (ARRL)
explanation: A club must have at least four members to receive a club station license grant [97.5(b)(2)]. The trustee does not need an Amateur Extra license and the club need not be registered with the ARRL.

question: Except for some specific restrictions, what is the maximum peak envelope power output for Technician class operators using frequencies above 30 MHz?
explanation: Above 30 MHz, Technicians may use up to 1500 watts PEP output, the same maximum as other license classes, except where specific band restrictions apply [97.313(b)]. The lower 200-watt limit applies only to their HF segments.

question: Which of the following is required when making on-the-air test transmissions?
optionB: Conduct tests only between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. local time
optionC: Notify the FCC of the transmissions
explanation: Test transmissions must be identified with your call sign just like any other transmission [97.119(a)]. There are no required test hours and no need to notify the FCC.

question: What is a common repeater frequency offset in the 2-meter band?
explanation: On the 2-meter band, repeaters commonly use an offset of plus or minus 600 kHz between their input and output frequencies. The 5 MHz offset is typical for 70 centimeters.

question: What is the purpose of the reverse function on a VHF/UHF transceiver?
optionC: To listen on a repeater’s input frequency
optionD: To listen on a repeater’s output frequency
explanation: The reverse function swaps your radio's transmit and receive frequencies so you can listen on the repeater's input frequency. This shows whether you can hear the other station directly and could move to simplex.

question: When do the FCC Part 97 Amateur Radio Service rules NOT apply to the operation of an amateur station?
explanation: FCC Part 97 rules always apply to an amateur station, including during RACES, ARES or other emergency operations [97.103(a)]. No organization's rules replace the FCC rules.

question: What is the national calling frequency for FM simplex operations in the 2-meter band?
explanation: 146.520 MHz is the national FM simplex calling frequency on 2 meters. 432.100 MHz and 446.000 MHz are in the 70-centimeter band, not 2 meters.

question: What term describes the use of a sub-audible tone transmitted along with normal voice audio to open the squelch of a receiver?
explanation: CTCSS (Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System) sends a low, sub-audible tone with your voice that opens the squelch of a receiver or repeater set for that tone. A tone burst is a short tone, not continuous, and DTMF is touch-tone signaling.

question: Which of the following are typical duties of a Net Control Station?
optionA: Choose the regular net meeting time and frequency
optionB: Ensure that all stations checking into the net are properly licensed for operation on the net frequency
optionC: Call the net to order and direct communications between stations checking in
explanation: A Net Control Station calls the net to order and directs the communications among stations that check in. It is not responsible for checking each station's license or setting the net schedule.

question: What is a common repeater frequency offset in the 70-centimeter band?
explanation: On the 70-centimeter band, repeaters commonly use an offset of plus or minus 5 MHz. The 600 kHz offset is typical of 2 meters.

question: Which of the following describes a linked repeater network?
optionA: A network of repeaters in which signals received by one repeater are transmitted by all the repeaters in the network
optionB: A single repeater with more than one receiver
optionC: Multiple repeaters with the same control operator
optionD: A system of repeaters linked by APRS
explanation: In a linked repeater network, a signal received by one repeater is retransmitted by all the repeaters in the network, extending coverage. It is not just a single repeater with several receivers or repeaters sharing a control operator.

question: What technique is used to ensure that voice messages containing unusual words are received correctly?
optionA: Send the words by voice and Morse code
optionB: Use the Q-code “QSR” to ask the receiving station to repeat the words back
optionC: Spell the words using a standard phonetic alphabet
explanation: Spelling unusual words with a standard phonetic alphabet (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie...) makes sure they are copied correctly. Morse code or Q-codes are not the standard technique for voice messages.

question: What is an appropriate way to call another station on a repeater if you know the other station's call sign?
optionA: Say "break, break," then the other station’s call sign, followed by your call sign
optionB: Say the station's call sign, then identify with your call sign
optionC: Say "CQ" three times, then the other station's call sign, followed by your call sign
optionD: Wait for the station to call CQ, then answer with your call sign
explanation: To call a known station on a repeater, say their call sign, then identify with your own call sign. "Break, break" is reserved for urgent or emergency traffic, and calling CQ is unnecessary when you know whom you want.

question: Which of the following could be the reason you are unable to access a repeater whose output you can hear?
optionB: You are using the wrong CTCSS tone
optionC: You are using the wrong DCS code
explanation: You can hear a repeater but still fail to open it if your transmit offset is wrong or you are not sending the CTCSS tone or DCS code it requires. Any of these will do it, so all choices are correct.

question: What is RACES?
optionA: An emergency organization combining amateur radio and citizens band operators and frequencies
optionC: A radio contest held in a short period, sometimes called a “sprint”
optionD: An FCC Part 97 amateur radio service for civil defense communications during national emergencies
explanation: RACES (Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service) is a Part 97 amateur radio service for civil defense communications during national emergencies. It does not involve citizens band operators or contests.

question: How should you respond to a station calling CQ?
optionA: Transmit "CQ" followed by the other station’s call sign
optionB: Transmit your call sign followed by the other station’s call sign
optionC: Transmit the other station’s call sign followed by your call sign
optionD: Transmit a signal report followed by your call sign
explanation: To answer a CQ, give the calling station's call sign first and then your own, so they know you are answering them. Repeating "CQ" yourself or giving your call first is not the normal reply.

question: Which of the following would cause your FM transmission audio to drop out on voice peaks?
optionB: Your FM deviation is too low
optionD: Your transmit power is too high
explanation: Talking too loudly causes over-deviation of your FM signal, which can make your audio drop out on voice peaks. Too little deviation would make you sound quiet, not cut out.

question: What does the term “traffic” refer to in net operation?
optionA: Formal messages exchanged by net stations
optionB: The number of stations checking in and out of a net
optionC: Operation by mobile or portable stations
optionD: A count of the number of activations of the net each month
explanation: In net operation, "traffic" means formal messages passed between stations on the net. It does not mean the count of check-ins or the number of mobile stations.

question: What is an effective way to seek a call from any phone station when not using a repeater?
optionA: Sign your call sign once, followed by the words “listening for a call;” if there is no answer, change the frequency and repeat
optionB: Say “QTC,” followed by “this is” and your call sign; if there is no answer, change the frequency and repeat
optionC: Transmit an unmodulated carrier for approximately 10 seconds, followed by “this is” and your call sign, and pause to listen; repeat as necessary
optionD: Repeat “CQ” a few times, followed by “this is,” and your call sign, then pause to listen; repeat as necessary
explanation: On a non-repeater phone frequency, you call "CQ" a few times, say "this is" and your call sign, then pause and listen for replies, repeating as needed. Sending an unmodulated carrier or using QTC is not a proper general call.

question: What type of signaling to a repeater uses two simultaneous audio tones?
explanation: DTMF (Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency) signaling, the same as telephone touch-tones, sends two audio tones at once for each key. CTCSS uses a single sub-audible tone.

question: What is the Amateur Radio Emergency Service (ARES)?
optionA: A group of licensed amateurs who have voluntarily registered their qualifications and equipment for communications duty in the public service
optionB: A group of licensed amateurs who are members of the military and who voluntarily agreed to provide message handling services in the case of an emergency
optionC: A training program that provides licensing courses for those interested in obtaining an amateur license to use during emergencies
optionD: A training program that certifies amateur operators for membership in the Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service
explanation: ARES is made up of licensed amateurs who voluntarily register their qualifications and equipment for public service communications duty. It is not a military group or a licensing or certification program.

question: What does the term "repeater offset" mean?
optionA: The difference between a repeater’s transmit and receive frequencies
optionB: The repeater has a time delay to prevent interference
optionC: The approximately half-second delay to allow for the “squelch tail” to be removed
optionD: The fee charged by the repeater owner or club to provide for maintenance
explanation: Repeater offset is the difference between a repeater's transmit (output) and receive (input) frequencies. It has nothing to do with time delays or fees.

question: How can you join a digital repeater’s “talkgroup”?
optionA: Register with the local Frequency Coordinator
optionB: Register with the digital repeater control operator
optionC: Program your radio with the group’s ID or code
optionD: Program your radio with the DTMF tone used by the talkgroup
explanation: To join a digital repeater talkgroup, you program your radio with that group's ID or code. No registration with a coordinator is needed, and DTMF tones are not used to select talkgroups.

question: Which of the following is standard practice when you participate in a net?
optionA: When first responding to the net control station, transmit your call sign, name, and address as in the FCC database
optionB: Record the time of each of your transmissions
optionC: Unless you are reporting an emergency, transmit only when directed by the net control station
explanation: In a directed net, you transmit only when the net control station calls on you, unless you have an emergency to report. Giving your full address or logging every transmission time is not standard practice.

question: What is the meaning of the procedural signal “CQ”?
optionA: A shortened form of the term “Contest QSO”
optionB: “Communication Quality,” used to indicate transmitted audio clarity
optionC: Only the called station should transmit
explanation: "CQ" means you are calling any station and inviting anyone to answer. It does not stand for "Contest QSO" or "Communication Quality."

question: Which of the following applies when two stations transmitting on the same frequency interfere with each other?
optionA: The stations should negotiate continued use of the frequency
optionB: Both stations should choose another frequency to avoid conflict
optionC: Whichever station was on the frequency first has preemptive rights to the frequency
optionD: Use subaudible tones so both stations can share the frequency
explanation: No station owns a frequency, so when two stations interfere with each other they should work out (negotiate) continued use of the frequency. Being there first does not give preemptive rights.

question: Which of the following relays messages using email addresses based on amateur callsigns?
explanation: Winlink is a system that relays email messages over radio using email addresses based on amateur call signs. FT8, PSK31 and AMTOR are digital modes, not email relay systems.

question: Which of the following is a customary way to indicate a station is listening on a repeater and looking for a contact?
optionA: “CQ CQ” followed by the repeater’s call sign
optionB: The station’s call sign followed by the word “listening”
optionC: The repeater’s call sign followed by the station’s call sign
explanation: On a repeater, the usual way to show you are available is to give your call sign followed by "listening." Calling CQ is common on simplex and HF but not customary on repeaters.

question: Why are simplex channels designated in the VHF/UHF band plans?
optionA: So stations within range of each other can communicate without tying up a repeater
optionD: So stations with simple transmitters can access the repeater without automated offset
explanation: Simplex channels are designated so stations within range of each other can talk directly without tying up a repeater. That leaves the repeater free for stations that actually need it.

question: Are amateur station control operators ever permitted to operate outside the frequency privileges of their license class?
optionB: Yes, but only when part of a FEMA emergency plan
optionC: Yes, but only when part of a RACES emergency plan
optionD: Yes, but only in situations involving the immediate safety of human life or protection of property
explanation: Yes, but only in situations involving the immediate safety of human life or protection of property, when an operator may use any means necessary to communicate. Being part of a FEMA or RACES plan does not by itself allow operating outside your privileges.

question: What is a band plan, beyond the privileges established by the FCC?
optionA: A voluntary guideline for using different modes or activities within an amateur band
optionC: A list of available net frequencies
optionD: A plan devised by a club to indicate frequency band usage
explanation: A band plan is a voluntary guideline, beyond the FCC rules, that suggests where different modes and activities should operate within a band. Following it helps avoid interference even though it is not law.

question: Which Q signal indicates that you are receiving interference from other stations?
explanation: QRM means interference from other stations or man-made sources. QRN, the most tempting distractor, means natural static or noise.

question: What information is contained in the preamble of a formal traffic message?
optionA: The email address of the originating station
optionB: The address of the intended recipient
optionC: The telephone number of the addressee
optionD: Information needed to track the message
explanation: The preamble of a formal message contains the information needed to track it, such as the message number, origin station, check, and date. The recipient's address and phone number are in a different part of the message.

question: What term describes an amateur station that is transmitting and receiving on the same frequency?
explanation: Simplex means transmitting and receiving on the same frequency, as when two stations talk directly without a repeater. Full duplex means transmitting and receiving at the same time, usually on separate frequencies.

question: Which Q signal indicates that you are changing frequency?
explanation: QSY means you are changing frequency (or asks another station to change). QSL means you acknowledge receipt, and QRZ asks who is calling.

question: What is meant by “check” in a radiogram header?
optionA: The number of words or word equivalents in the text portion of the message
optionB: The call sign of the originating station
optionC: A list of stations that have relayed the message
optionD: A box on the message form that indicates that the message was received and/or relayed
explanation: In a radiogram, the "check" is the number of words or word equivalents in the message text, which helps the receiving station confirm nothing was lost. It is not a list of relaying stations or a received box.

question: What is the digital color code used on DMR repeater systems?
optionA: An access code which must be programmed into a DMR transmitter to access a specific repeater
optionB: A code which automatically programs the repeater offset to a frequency chosen by the user
optionC: A code which identifies the specific CODEC being used so that the repeater can properly decode the audio
optionD: A code transmitted by the repeater to indicate health and status of the equipment
explanation: A DMR color code is an access code that must be programmed into your DMR radio to access a specific repeater, similar to a CTCSS tone on analog FM. It does not set offsets or report equipment status.

question: Which of the following requires certification by a civil defense agency?
explanation: RACES requires certification by a civil defense agency for its operators [97.407(a)]. ARES and SKYWARN are volunteer programs that do not require civil defense certification.

question: What is the purpose of a squelch function?
optionA: Reduce a CW transmitter's key clicks
optionB: Mute the receiver audio when a signal is not present
optionC: Eliminate parasitic oscillations in an RF amplifier
explanation: Squelch mutes the receiver's audio when no signal is present, so you do not hear constant background noise. It does not reduce key clicks, oscillations or impulse noise.

question: Which of the following is a “talkgroup”?
optionA: A group of amateur radio operators who share email on a specific amateur radio topic
optionB: An identifier used by DMR to organize radio traffic so that those who want to hear the group aren’t bothered by other radio traffic
optionC: The members of a net organized for amateur radio operators with a specific common interest
optionD: A method of automatically alerting all group members to the frequency where any member is transmitting
explanation: A talkgroup is a DMR identifier that organizes traffic so users hear only the group they want and are not bothered by other traffic. It is a digital radio feature, not an email list or a net.

question: Why do VHF signal strengths sometimes vary greatly when the antenna is moved only a few feet?
optionA: The signal path encounters different concentrations of water vapor
optionB: VHF ionospheric propagation is very sensitive to path length
optionC: Multipath propagation cancels or reinforces signals
optionD: The Doppler effect causes slight frequency shifts which result in changes in signal strength
explanation: At VHF a signal often reaches you by several paths at once, direct plus reflections off buildings and terrain, and moving the antenna a few feet changes how those copies line up. Where they arrive in phase they reinforce and where they arrive out of phase they cancel, which is multipath. VHF line of sight signals are not normally carried by the ionosphere, so ionospheric path length is not the cause.

question: What is the relationship between the electric and magnetic fields of an electromagnetic wave?
explanation: A radio wave is made of an electric field and a magnetic field that are perpendicular (at 90 degrees) to each other and to the direction the wave travels. Both fields travel together at the same speed.

question: Why are simplex UHF signals rarely heard beyond their radio horizon?
optionA: They are too weak to go very far
optionB: FCC regulations prohibit them from going more than 50 miles
optionC: UHF signals are usually not propagated by the ionosphere
optionD: UHF signals are absorbed by the ionospheric D region
explanation: UHF signals normally pass right through the ionosphere instead of being bent back to Earth, so simplex UHF contacts are mostly limited to line of sight, about to the radio horizon. FCC rules set no distance limit, and D region absorption mainly affects lower HF frequencies.

question: How does vegetation affect UHF and microwave signals?
optionA: Causes knife-edge diffraction, distorting voice peaks
optionB: Absorbs signals, leading to poor reception of weak signals
optionC: Amplifies signals, improving reception of weak signals
explanation: Leaves, branches and other vegetation contain water that absorbs UHF and microwave energy, so a path through trees weakens the signal. That loss matters most for signals that were already weak, which may disappear entirely.

question: What property of a radio wave defines its polarization?
optionA: The orientation of the electric field
optionB: The orientation of the magnetic field
optionC: The ratio of the energy in the magnetic field to the energy in the electric field
optionD: The ratio of the velocity to the wavelength
explanation: By definition, a radio wave's polarization is the direction of its electric field. A vertical antenna produces a vertical electric field, so its signal is vertically polarized.

question: What is a characteristic of HF communication compared with communications on VHF and higher frequencies?
optionC: Long-distance ionospheric propagation is far more common on HF
optionD: There is less atmospheric interference (static) on HF
explanation: HF frequencies (3 to 30 MHz) are regularly refracted by the ionosphere, so long-distance skywave contacts are far more common on HF than on VHF and higher bands. HF actually has more atmospheric static and needs larger antennas, not smaller ones.

question: What antenna polarization is normally used for long-distance CW and SSB contacts on the VHF and UHF bands?
explanation: By convention, long-distance (weak signal) CW and SSB work on VHF and UHF uses horizontal polarization, typically with horizontal Yagis. FM and repeater work uses vertical polarization instead, so the two groups would lose signal strength if they mixed.

question: What are the two components of a radio wave?
explanation: An electromagnetic (radio) wave consists of an electric field and a magnetic field oscillating together. Voltage and current exist in the antenna and feed line, not in the wave traveling through space.

question: What is one characteristic of VHF signals received via auroral backscatter?
optionA: They are often received from 10,000 miles or more
optionB: They are distorted, with a characteristic raspy sound
optionC: They occur only during winter nighttime hours
optionD: They are generally strongest when your antenna is aimed west
explanation: Auroral signals are scattered by moving, ionized curtains of the aurora, which spreads and distorts them and gives a characteristic raspy, buzzing sound. Stations usually aim toward the aurora (north in the Northern Hemisphere), not west.

question: What is the effect of antenna cross-polarization over a line-of-sight VHF or UHF path?
explanation: If one station's antenna is vertical and the other's is horizontal, the receiving antenna picks up only a small part of the arriving wave, so the received signal is much weaker. Over a direct line of sight path the loss can be large, which is why FM and repeater users all stick to vertical polarization.

question: What is the velocity of a radio wave traveling through free space?
explanation: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves, like light, so in free space they travel at the speed of light, about 300,000,000 meters per second. The 0.86 figure resembles a feed line velocity factor, which applies inside cable, not in free space.

question: Which of the following types of propagation is most commonly associated with occasional strong signals on the 10-, 6-, and 2-meter bands from beyond the radio horizon?
explanation: Sporadic E occurs when patches of the E region become dense enough to reflect 10, 6 and sometimes 2 meter signals, producing sudden strong signals from hundreds to over a thousand miles away. It is occasional and unpredictable, most common in late spring and summer.

question: When using a directional antenna, how might your station be able to communicate with a distant repeater if buildings or obstructions are blocking the direct line of sight path?
optionA: Change from vertical to horizontal polarization
optionB: Try to find a path that reflects signals to the repeater
explanation: A directional antenna can be aimed at a building, hill or other surface that bounces the signal toward the repeater, going around the obstruction. Raising SWR or swapping polarization would only weaken the signal, and long path is an HF ionospheric idea.

question: What is the relationship between wavelength and frequency?
optionA: Wavelength gets longer as frequency increases
optionB: Wavelength gets shorter as frequency increases
optionC: Wavelength is constant at all frequencies
optionD: Wavelength and frequency increase as path length increases
explanation: Wavelength and frequency are inversely related: wavelength = speed of light / frequency, so as frequency goes up, wavelength gets shorter. For example, 3.5 MHz is about 80 meters while 146 MHz is about 2 meters.

question: Which of the following effects may allow radio signals to travel beyond obstructions between the transmitting and receiving stations?
explanation: Knife-edge diffraction lets a radio wave bend around a sharp edge such as a mountain ridge or building top, so some signal reaches stations hidden behind the obstruction. Doppler shift and Faraday rotation change frequency or polarization and do not get a signal around obstacles.

question: What is the meaning of the term “picket fencing”?
optionA: Alternating transmissions during a net operation
optionB: Rapid flutter on mobile signals due to multipath propagation
optionC: A type of ground system used with vertical antennas
optionD: Interference from cable TV in the form of carriers at fixed intervals across the band
explanation: Picket fencing is the rapid flutter heard on a mobile VHF or UHF signal as the vehicle moves through spots where reflected signals alternately reinforce and cancel. It is a multipath effect, named for the sound of running a stick along a picket fence.

question: What is the formula for converting frequency to approximate wavelength in meters?
optionA: Wavelength in meters equals frequency in hertz multiplied by 300
optionB: Wavelength in meters equals frequency in hertz divided by 300
optionC: Wavelength in meters equals frequency in megahertz divided by 300
optionD: Wavelength in meters equals 300 divided by frequency in megahertz
explanation: Wavelength in meters is approximately 300 divided by the frequency in megahertz, because the speed of light is about 300 million meters per second. For example, 300 / 146 MHz gives about 2 meters.

question: What type of propagation is responsible for allowing over-the-horizon VHF and UHF communications to ranges of approximately 300 miles on a regular basis?
explanation: Tropospheric ducting traps VHF and UHF signals between layers of air with different temperature and humidity, guiding them far beyond line of sight, often around 300 miles. It happens in the lower atmosphere, while D and F2 region effects are ionospheric and mostly influence HF.

question: What weather condition might decrease range at microwave frequencies?
explanation: At microwave frequencies the wavelength is short enough that rain, snow and other precipitation absorb and scatter the signal, shortening the usable range. Wind and pressure changes have no direct effect on the radio wave itself.

question: In addition to frequency, which of the following is used to identify amateur radio bands?
explanation: Amateur bands are commonly named by their approximate wavelength, such as the 20 meter, 2 meter or 70 centimeter band. Channel numbers and letter designators are not the usual amateur naming system.

question: What band is best suited for communicating via meteor scatter?
explanation: Meteor trails leave brief streaks of ionized gas that reflect signals best at lower VHF, which makes 6 meters the best amateur band for meteor scatter. Higher bands such as 2 meters and 70 cm also work but with shorter, weaker reflections.

question: What is a likely cause of irregular fading of signals propagated by the ionosphere?
optionA: Frequency shift due to Faraday rotation
optionD: Random combining of signals arriving via different paths
explanation: A signal reflected by the ionosphere usually arrives over several slightly different paths whose lengths keep shifting as the ionosphere moves. As those copies randomly add and cancel, the received signal fades up and down irregularly.

question: What frequency range is referred to as VHF?
explanation: VHF (Very High Frequency) covers 30 MHz to 300 MHz, which includes the 6 meter, 2 meter and 1.25 meter amateur bands. Radio ranges go up by factors of ten: HF is 3 to 30 MHz, VHF 30 to 300 MHz and UHF 300 to 3000 MHz.

question: What causes tropospheric ducting?
optionA: Discharges of lightning during electrical storms
explanation: A temperature inversion, where a layer of warm air sits above cooler air, bends VHF and UHF signals back down and creates a duct that carries them far beyond the horizon. Lightning and sunspots have nothing to do with this lower-atmosphere effect.

question: Which of the following results from the fact that signals propagated by the ionosphere are elliptically polarized?
optionB: Either vertically or horizontally polarized antennas may be used for transmission or reception
optionD: Both the transmitting and receiving antennas must be of the same polarization
explanation: The ionosphere twists and mixes the polarization of a signal, so it arrives elliptically polarized with both vertical and horizontal components. That means for HF skywave contacts either a vertical or a horizontal antenna works, and the two stations need not match.

question: What frequency range is referred to as UHF?
explanation: UHF (Ultra High Frequency) covers 300 MHz to 3000 MHz, which includes the 70 cm, 33 cm and 23 cm amateur bands. It is the decade just above VHF (30 to 300 MHz).

question: What is generally the best time for long-distance 10-meter band propagation via the F region?
optionA: From dawn to shortly after sunset during periods of high sunspot activity
optionB: From shortly after sunset to dawn during periods of high sunspot activity
optionC: From dawn to shortly after sunset during periods of low sunspot activity
optionD: From shortly after sunset to dawn during periods of low sunspot activity
explanation: The F region is ionized by sunlight, so 10 meter skip is best during daylight, from dawn to shortly after sunset. It needs high sunspot activity to ionize the F region strongly enough to reflect frequencies as high as 28 MHz.

question: What effect does multi-path propagation have on data transmissions?
optionA: Transmission rates must be increased by a factor equal to the number of separate paths observed
optionB: Transmission rates must be decreased by a factor equal to the number of separate paths observed
optionC: No significant changes will occur if the signals are transmitted using FM
optionD: Error rates are likely to increase
explanation: When several delayed copies of a data signal arrive, the echoes smear the symbols into one another and confuse the decoder, so more bits are received wrong. Switching to FM does not fix this, and the data rate does not change by a factor of the number of paths.

question: What frequency range is referred to as HF?
explanation: HF (High Frequency) covers 3 MHz to 30 MHz, home of the bands from 80 meters through 10 meters where ionospheric skip is common. The range 300 to 3000 kHz is MF (medium frequency), one decade lower.

question: Which of the following bands may provide long-distance communications via the ionosphere’s F region during the peak of the sunspot cycle?
explanation: Near the peak of the sunspot cycle the F region can become ionized enough to reflect 10 meter and even 6 meter signals for worldwide contacts. Bands at 1.25 meters and higher (including 70 cm and 23 cm) essentially always pass through the ionosphere.

question: Which region of the atmosphere can reflect HF radio waves?
explanation: The ionosphere is the ionized upper atmosphere, starting roughly 50 km (30 miles) up, and it bends (refracts) HF signals back toward Earth, allowing skywave contacts far beyond the horizon. The troposphere is the lower weather layer, which affects VHF and higher but does not return HF signals.

question: What is the approximate velocity of a radio wave in free space?
explanation: Radio waves in free space travel at the speed of light, about 300,000,000 meters per second (3 x 10^8 m/s). This is the number behind the rule wavelength in meters = 300 / frequency in MHz.

question: Why is the radio horizon for VHF and UHF signals more distant than the visual horizon?
optionA: Radio signals move somewhat faster than the speed of light
optionB: Radio waves are not blocked by dust particles
optionC: The atmosphere refracts radio waves slightly
optionD: Radio waves are blocked by dust particles
explanation: The atmosphere gets thinner with height, which bends (refracts) radio waves slightly back toward the curved Earth, so the radio horizon is about 15 percent farther than the visual horizon. Radio waves do not travel faster than light.

question: What effect does fog or rain have on 10-meter and 6-meter band signals?
explanation: At 10 and 6 meters the wavelength (about 10 m and 6 m) is far larger than raindrops, so fog and rain have little effect on the signal. Rain absorption becomes a real problem only at microwave frequencies.

question: Which of these frequencies travels at the highest velocity in free space?
optionD: All radio frequencies travel at the same velocity
explanation: All electromagnetic waves, whatever their frequency, travel at the speed of light in free space. Higher frequency changes the wavelength, not the speed.

question: Which of the following is an appropriate power supply rating for a typical 50-watt output mobile FM transceiver?
explanation: Mobile radios run from a nominal 12 volt vehicle system, specified as 13.8 V, and a 50 watt FM transmitter draws roughly 10 amperes or more, so a 13.8 V, 12 A supply fits. A 4 A supply would sag or shut down on transmit, and 24 V would damage the radio.

question: What is the effect of excessive microphone gain on SSB transmissions?
explanation: Too much microphone gain overdrives the SSB transmitter, causing clipped, distorted audio and splatter onto nearby frequencies. It does not change frequency stability or SWR.

question: Which of the following should be considered when selecting an accessory SWR meter?
optionA: The frequency and power level at which the measurements will be made
optionB: The distance that the meter will be located from the antenna
optionC: The maximum SWR anticipated on the transmission line
optionD: The ability of the meter to compensate for a poor transmission line match to the antenna
explanation: An SWR meter is designed for a particular frequency range and maximum power, so you must choose one rated for the bands and power you will use. A meter only measures SWR; it cannot compensate for a poor antenna match.

question: Which of the following can be used to enter a transceiver’s operating frequency?
explanation: Most transceivers let you enter a frequency directly on the keypad or tune to it with the VFO (variable frequency oscillator) knob. CTCSS and DTMF are tone signals, not ways to set the operating frequency.

question: Why are short, heavy-gauge wires used for a transceiver’s DC power connection?
optionA: To minimize voltage drop when transmitting
optionB: To provide a close match to the power supply output impedance
optionD: To minimize radiative losses in the power cable
explanation: A transceiver draws high current when transmitting, and any wire resistance causes a voltage drop (V = I x R). Short, thick wire has low resistance, so the radio still gets close to full supply voltage at full power.

question: How is squelch adjusted so that a weak FM signal can be heard?
optionA: Set the squelch threshold so that receiver output audio is on all the time
optionB: Turn up the audio level until it overcomes the squelch threshold
explanation: Squelch mutes the receiver until the signal is above a threshold, so a very weak signal may never open it. Turning squelch down until the audio stays on all the time (you hear background noise) lets the weakest signals through. Turning up the volume does nothing while the squelch is closed.

question: How are the audio input and output of a transceiver connected in a station configured to operate using FT8?
optionA: To a computer running a terminal program and connected to a terminal node controller unit
optionB: To the audio output and input of a computer running FT8 software
optionC: To an FT8 conversion unit, a keyboard, and a computer monitor
optionD: To a computer connected to the FT8converter.com website
explanation: FT8 is a sound card mode: the radio's receive audio goes to the computer's audio input for decoding, and the computer's audio output feeds the radio's transmit audio. No terminal node controller or special converter box is required, just a computer running FT8 software.

question: What does an FM signal sound like when received slightly off frequency?
optionC: There is no effect except for reduction in amplitude
explanation: An FM receiver tuned slightly off frequency no longer centers the signal in its passband, so the recovered audio becomes distorted. Unlike SSB, FM does not shift in pitch when mistuned.

question: Where should an RF power meter be installed?
optionA: In the feed line, between the transmitter and antenna
optionC: In parallel with the push-to-talk line and the antenna
optionD: In the power supply cable, as close as possible to the radio
explanation: An RF power meter measures power flowing to the antenna, so it is inserted in the feed line between transmitter and antenna. The power supply cable carries DC, not RF, so a meter there would not measure transmitted RF power.

question: What does the scanning function of an FM transceiver do?
optionC: Tunes through a range of frequencies to check for activity
optionD: Tunes through a range of frequencies to determine the antenna’s resonant frequency
explanation: Scanning automatically steps the receiver through a range of frequencies or memory channels, stopping when it finds activity. It does not measure deviation or antenna resonance.

question: What signals are used in a computer-radio interface for digital mode operation?
optionA: Receive and transmit mode, status, and location
optionC: Receive audio, transmit audio, and transmitter keying
optionD: NMEA GPS location and DC power
explanation: A computer-radio interface for digital modes passes receive audio from the radio to the computer, transmit audio from the computer to the radio, and a keying signal (PTT) to switch the radio into transmit. RF power and the antenna do not pass through the interface.

question: Which of the following controls could be used if the voice pitch of a single-sideband signal returning to your CQ call seems too high or low?
explanation: RIT (Receiver Incremental Tuning), also called the Clarifier, shifts only the receive frequency slightly so a mistuned SSB voice sounds natural, without moving your transmit frequency. Tone squelch and AGC do not change the pitch of SSB audio.

question: Which of the following is one of the connections required between a computer and a transceiver to operate digital modes?
optionC: Computer “line in” to transceiver speaker connector
optionD: Computer “line out” to transceiver speaker connector
explanation: The computer listens to the radio, so the transceiver's speaker or audio output connects to the computer's line in. Line out goes to the radio's microphone or data input, not to push-to-talk, which needs a separate keying signal.

question: What is a DMR “code plug”?
optionA: An adapter cable used to connect a DMR radio to a computer for internet access
optionB: Configuration data loaded onto your radio to access repeaters and talkgroups
optionC: An upgrade to DMR programming software provided by the radio manufacturer to accommodate new radio models
optionD: A Coder-Decoder (CODEC) that converts analog voice data to DMR digital data and vice versa
explanation: A DMR code plug is the configuration file (channels, frequencies, talkgroups, color codes and your ID) that is programmed into the radio so it can access repeaters and talkgroups. Despite the name, it is data, not a physical plug or adapter.

question: Which of the following conductors is preferred for bonding at RF?
optionA: Copper braid removed from coaxial cable
explanation: Flat copper strap has a large surface area and low inductance at radio frequencies, because RF current flows on the surface of a conductor. Braid salvaged from coax is a tempting choice, but it corrodes and its loose strands make it a poorer RF bond.

question: What is the advantage of having a choice of receiver filter bandwidths in a multimode transceiver?
optionA: Permits monitoring several modes simultaneously by selecting a separate filter for each mode
optionB: Permits noise or interference reduction by selecting a bandwidth matching the mode
optionC: Increases the number of frequencies that can be stored in memory
optionD: Increases the amount of offset between receive and transmit frequencies
explanation: Choosing a receive filter about as wide as the signal, narrow for CW and wider for SSB, lets the signal through while rejecting noise and nearby interference. A filter that is too wide admits extra noise for no benefit.

question: How can you determine the length of time that equipment can be powered from a battery?
optionA: Divide the watt-hour rating of the battery by the peak power consumption of the equipment
optionB: Divide the battery ampere-hour rating by the average current draw of the equipment
optionC: Multiply the watts per hour consumed by the equipment by the battery power rating
optionD: Multiply the square of the current rating of the battery by the input resistance of the equipment
explanation: Operating time in hours is approximately the battery capacity in ampere-hours divided by the equipment's average current draw. For example, a 20 Ah battery powering gear that averages 2 A lasts about 20 / 2 = 10 hours. Using peak power instead of average draw would underestimate the run time.

question: How is a specific group of stations selected on a DMR digital voice transceiver?
optionA: By retrieving the frequencies from transceiver memory
optionB: By enabling the group’s CTCSS tone
optionC: By entering the group’s identification code
optionD: By inserting a five-pin, pre-programmed code plug
explanation: On DMR, a talkgroup is selected by its identification number (talkgroup ID), entered or chosen in the radio's programming. CTCSS tones are an analog FM feature, and a code plug is a data file, not a physical five-pin plug.

question: What function does a digital mode hotspot perform for nearby transceivers?
optionA: Communication with a digital voice or data network
optionB: FT8 digital communications via AFSK using a smartphone connected to the internet
optionC: RTTY encoding and decoding without a computer
optionD: High-speed digital communications for meteor scatter
explanation: A digital mode hotspot is a small low-power radio linked to the internet that lets nearby digital voice radios (such as DMR or D-STAR) connect to a digital voice or data network. It is a gateway, not an FT8, RTTY or meteor scatter device.

question: Which of the following receiver filter bandwidths provides the best signal-to-noise ratio for SSB reception?
explanation: An SSB voice signal is about 2400 to 3000 Hz wide, so a 2400 Hz filter passes the voice while rejecting extra noise. A 500 Hz filter suits CW and would cut off much of the voice, while 5000 Hz admits unnecessary noise.

question: Where should the negative power return of a mobile transceiver be connected in a vehicle?
optionB: To the shell of the power connector
optionC: To any metal part of the vehicle
explanation: Run the negative lead to the vehicle battery's negative terminal, where it connects to chassis ground, so the radio's high current does not flow through random paths in the car body. Connecting to just any metal part can add resistance and pick up noise from other vehicle systems.

question: Which of the following must be programmed into a D-STAR digital transceiver before transmitting?
explanation: D-STAR transmits your call sign digitally in every transmission, so the radio must be programmed with your call sign before you transmit. Output power and codec type do not need to be set first.

question: What is an electronic keyer?
optionA: A device for switching antennas from transmit to receive
optionB: A device for voice activated switching from receive to transmit
optionC: A device that assists in manual sending of Morse code
optionD: An interlock to prevent unauthorized use of a radio
explanation: An electronic keyer helps you send Morse code manually by automatically forming correctly timed dots and dashes when you press a paddle. Switching from receive to transmit by voice is VOX, which is a different function.

question: Electrical current is measured in which of the following units?
explanation: Current, the flow of electric charge, is measured in amperes (amps). Volts measure voltage, ohms measure resistance and watts measure power.

question: How many milliamperes is 1.5 amperes?
explanation: Milli means one thousandth, so there are 1000 milliamperes in an ampere. 1.5 A x 1000 = 1500 mA.

question: What describes the ability to store energy in an electric field?
explanation: Capacitance is the ability to store energy in an electric field, such as the field between the plates of a capacitor. Inductance is the related property that stores energy in a magnetic field instead.

question: What formula is used to calculate current in a circuit?
explanation: Ohm's law, rearranged for current, is I = E / R: current equals voltage divided by resistance. More voltage pushes more current, and more resistance allows less.

question: Electrical power is measured in which of the following units?
